summary: Defines a TSIG algorithm based on the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API, RFC 2743). TSIG gives transaction-level authentication for DNS, and this makes it extensible with GSS-based keys. It updates RFC 2845 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: DNS replies can be faked. A secret handshake lets two computers prove who they are. This document lets them use a bigger, shared security toolbox to do the handshake.

subtitle: How DNS clients and servers use GSS-API security mechanisms such as Kerberos to sign their messages with TSIG.

tldr.problem: TSIG authenticates DNS messages and can be extended with new algorithms, but there was no algorithm that let DNS reuse an existing security infrastructure such as Kerberos instead of managing its own keys.
tldr.mechanism: The gss-tsig algorithm uses GSS-API calls to negotiate a security context, carrying the opaque tokens in TKEY records. Once the context exists, GSS_GetMIC and GSS_VerifyMIC produce and check the signatures in TSIG records.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2845 so a server may sign its response to an unsigned TKEY query. The protection is only as strong as the underlying GSS mechanism.

facts.label: Required mechanism
facts.value: Kerberos v5 (clients), SPNEGO and Kerberos v5 (servers)

today: RFC 3645 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2003. It updates RFC 2845, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why TSIG Needs GSS-API
sections.content:
TSIG (RFC 2845) gives DNS messages lightweight authentication and integrity between two DNS entities, such as a client and a server or two servers. It can protect dynamic updates, authenticate regular messages, or let a client offload complicated DNSSEC processing to a server and still trust the answers.

TSIG can be extended with new algorithms. This RFC defines one based on the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API, RFC 2743), a framework that hides security details from the protocol designer. Its benefits are mechanism independence (for example Kerberos for one transaction and SPKM for another client) and not having to build a new key distribution or key management system.

The scope is authentication only. The document does not propose an authorization mechanism.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a brand new lock for every door, DNS borrows a toolbox of locks that already exists. The toolbox decides which lock to use.

sections.title: Algorithm Overview
sections.content:
Client and server create a security context, which is then used to create and verify signatures on their messages. A unique context is required for each unique connection between a client and a server, and a context has a finite lifetime. Every connection starts in the uninitialized state, then moves to negotiating and finally to established.

The algorithm has two stages. First the client and server call GSS_Init_sec_context and GSS_Accept_sec_context to generate tokens, which they pass to each other using TKEY (RFC 2930) as the transport. Second, the established context generates and verifies signatures with GSS_GetMIC and GSS_VerifyMIC, and these signatures travel in TSIG records. Both sides MUST already be locally authenticated and hold default credentials.

The RFC also changes one rule in RFC 2845 section 4.2. The old text said a server must not sign a response to an unsigned request. The new text makes an exception for a response to an unsigned TKEY query once the secret key is established on the server, provided the key establishment algorithm explicitly says so.
sections.eli5: First the two computers swap secret notes until they trust each other. Then they stamp every message with a seal only they can make.

sections.title: Negotiating the Context
sections.content:
The client calls GSS_Init_sec_context with its flags for replay detection, mutual authentication, delegation, sequencing and integrity set to TRUE and anonymity set to FALSE. The target name is DNS@<target_server_name>. If the call returns one of the listed error statuses, the client MUST abandon GSS-TSIG for that context. If the call completes but replay detection or mutual authentication is not provided, the client MUST also abandon the algorithm.

The output token goes to the server in a query with QTYPE=TKEY, in the Key Data field of a TKEY record in the additional section. On the server side, a TKEY query whose Mode is 3 and Algorithm Name is gss-tsig is looked up by key name. A new name starts a negotiation; an established, unexpired context gets a BADNAME error in the TKEY error field; an expired one is deleted and a new negotiation begins.

The server calls GSS_Accept_sec_context and answers with RCODE NOERROR and a TKEY record in the answer section. Failure statuses set the TKEY error field to BADKEY. On GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED the server returns its token and the exchange continues. On GSS_S_COMPLETE the server signs the response with TSIG and the context is established. Both sides MUST limit the number of attempts or continuations to prevent endless looping, with ten as the ceiling.

When finished, the client SHOULD delete its context and ask the server to delete its own by sending a TKEY record with Mode 5, key deletion. A server may end a context at any time and may hint at this with the same Mode 5 record.
sections.eli5: The client and server pass notes back and forth until both are happy. If anything looks wrong they stop, and they are only allowed to try so many times so they never go around in circles forever.

sections.title: The TKEY and TSIG Records
sections.content:
A client-sent TKEY record has a NAME that is a client-generated, globally unique domain name string. This name is the key name that identifies the security context to both sides, so the client SHOULD make it globally unique, and it MAY contain a UUID/GUID. The RDATA carries gss-tsig as the Algorithm Name, Mode 3 (GSS-API negotiation), a Key Size equal to the token size in octets, and the token itself as Key Data. The other fields are set as RFC 2930 describes.

For signed messages the TSIG record uses the key name of the context as its NAME and gss-tsig as the Algorithm Name. The remaining fields follow RFC 2845. Client and server each keep a mapping table: the client maps (target_name, key_name, context_handle) and the server maps (key_name, context_handle).
sections.eli5: Each handshake gets a one-of-a-kind label so both sides know which conversation a note belongs to. The label is written on every note and every seal.

sections.title: Signing and Verifying Messages
sections.content:
To sign, the sender passes the whole DNS message plus the TSIG variables to GSS_GetMIC with a default QOP of 0. The returned token goes in the Signature field of the TSIG record. If the status shows the context or credentials expired, or a failure, the caller MUST delete the context and SHOULD negotiate a new one. For GSS_S_NO_CONTEXT the entry is also removed from the mapping table. For GSS_S_BAD_QOP the caller SHOULD retry with an allowed value, within a limit.

To verify, the TSIG record NAME selects the context. If it does not map to an established context, the server MUST send a standard TSIG error response with BADKEY. Otherwise GSS_VerifyMIC checks the Signature field. Even when the signature is authentic, the timer values in the TSIG record MUST also be valid, and the caller MUST NOT act on the message until both checks pass. Several failure statuses, such as a bad signature or an old or duplicate token, make the server answer with a TSIG BADKEY error.
sections.eli5: Every message gets a seal made from the shared secret. The receiver checks the seal and the time on it, and ignores the message if either looks wrong.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a client client.example.com and a server server.example.com. The client calls GSS_Init_sec_context for DNS@server.example.com, gets GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED and a token, and sends a TKEY query for the key name 789.client.example.com.server.example.com..

The server does not find that name in its table, calls GSS_Accept_sec_context, stores the new handle and replies with its own token. The client calls GSS_Init_sec_context again, gets GSS_S_COMPLETE with a non-NULL token, and sends one more TKEY query. The server completes with a NULL token, so it echoes the client's TKEY record in the answer section and adds a TSIG record signed with GSS_GetMIC. The client verifies that signature with GSS_VerifyMIC and the context is established on both sides.
sections.eli5: The client knocks, the server answers, the client replies once more, and then the server shows a signed note to prove it is really the server.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The protocol is only as secure as the underlying GSS mechanisms. All security considerations from RFC 2845, RFC 2930 and RFC 2743 also apply.

If a response that should be signed is unsigned or has an invalid signature, the RFC says an attacker has tampered with it or tried to send the client a false response. The client MAY then keep waiting for another answer to the same query until a locally configured time runs out. The RFC calls this a new option that lets a client accept multiple answers for one query ID and pick one by some criteria. IANA has reserved the TSIG algorithm name gss-tsig for the Algorithm fields of TKEY and TSIG records.
sections.eli5: A lock is only as good as the toolbox it came from. If a note arrives without a good seal, the client knows someone may be faking it and keeps waiting for the real one.

sections.title: Conformance and Interoperability
sections.content:
GSS-API with SPNEGO (RFC 2478) lets client and server negotiate the underlying security mechanism on the fly, so DNS clients and servers SHOULD specify the SPNEGO mech_type. To guarantee interoperability, DNS servers are required to specify SPNEGO, the GSS-API used by a client must support Kerberos v5, and the GSS-API used by a server must support both SPNEGO and Kerberos v5.

Implementations MAY also support other underlying mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees that at least one common lock, Kerberos, must always be in the toolbox, so two different computers can always find a lock they both know.
